newsitem.title: UK: Buba concern about dlr rise overstated - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Buba concern about dlr rise overstated - analysts.

text.p: Bundesbank concern about the inflationary impact of a rising dollar/mark may be overstated and the impact of the dollar's recent rise on the real German economy may be less than many in the market now assume, analysts say.

As a result, Bundesbank protestations about further sharp gains in dollar/mark are merely a traditional rebuke of what they see as potential instability and volatility and have little or nothing to do with the level of the dollar.

Analysts argue dollar/mark may be forced to take the burden of a further, and many say necessary, mark depreciation because the advent of European monetary union will prevent mark losses against the currencies of its biggest trading partners.
"Long-term, the concern about the inflationary impact of the dollar's rise on Germany is a complete red herring," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
"The Bundesbank just does not like what its sees as FX instability. It is not the level of the dollar."

The Bundesbank's repeated assertion over the past week that exchange rates have fully corrected the distortions of early 1995 has come at a time when the mark's slide so far this year has been almost exclusively against the dollar and sterling.
Since the start of 1997, the mark has lost about 10 percent against the dollar and about six percent against the pound.

Collectively these two currencies account for just 21.5 percent of the mark's trade-weighted index - an index derived from the relative proportion of trade in manufactured goods which Germany has with its major trading partners.
On the other hand, the proportion of the mark's trade-weighted basket held by the quasi-mark currencies of Austria, Belgium and the Netherlands is also 21 percent.
The mark is closely pegged to these currencies and, true to form, has barely moved against them over the past year.
Add the French franc, which has been little changed against the mark this year, the proportion of the mark's trade weighted index unaffected this year rises to just over 37 percent.
The volatile lira and peseta, meantime, together account for 17.5 percent of the mark index. Net movements in these currencies on the mark in 1997 have not exceeeded 0.5 percent.

As a result, the major mark slide against sterling and the dollar, which together account for 21 percent of its trade-weighted index, stacks up against virtually no move in a basket of currencies which account for 55 percent of the mark's basket.
One caveat is the dollar's role in denominating international trade in oil of which German is large importer.
But, analysts say this is just a denominational effect and the price of oil typically moves inversely to the dollar itself.
Brent crude oil futures are down 17 percent so far this year and this more than offsets the 10 percent rise in dollar/mark.

In any event, the Bundesbank has said the dollar/mark had corrected, or "normalised" in its favoured parlance, at 1.65. This suggests it has been unperturbed by its move to that level at least and, to date, the dollar has only risen 2.6 percent from this perceived "normal" level.
So why is the Bundesbank so irritated?

"What the Bundesbank is worried about is that the pace of the dollar/mark move was unsettling and the dollar is entering a potentially explosive phase," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"In that environment, it needed to act now, not because it cares about 1.70 but because it knows that the market could easily power this to 1.85 in a matter of weeks," said Meggyesi.
Analysts say the potential for a dollar/mark "overshoot" is high because of the make up of its exchange rate index.

"If you assume European monetary union will keep the mark stable on its Euro cross rates, then dollar/mark will have to accelerate far higher to provide Germany with the sort of economic impulse it needs from exchange rate depreciation," said Tony Norfield, treasury econmist at ABN Amro.
The overshoot idea is attractive to others too.

"The damage inflicted by Europe's overvalued exchange rates has become so deeply ingrained that it will likely take more than just a return to exchange rate equilibrium or fair-value exchange rates(to correct it)" said Michael Rosenberg, head of Merrill Lynch international fixed income research in New York.
Rosenberg, in a note to clients, said he expects dollar to reach 1.80 marks by the end of 1997 and 2.00 by the year 2000.
Von Maydell at UBS said mark weakness may be cyclical but the cycle goes back to German reunificantion in 1990.

He said the mark's peak reached four-to-five years after that was a product of the subsequent German policy mix and was similiar to the dollar surge in the mid-1980's based on the policies of ex-U.S. president Ronald Reagan.

Estimates of a full unwinding of this period of mark strength, crucially against a backdrop of EMU in Europe, could lead to the dollar/mark overshooting to as high as 2.35 in ther years ahead, said Von Maydell.
